## Cool flex AI bro

I am tickled by reports that, among elite AI researchers, cigarettes are back.

The logic goes like this:

If you really believe in AI and that AI will hit recursive self-improvement and achieve super-intelligence,

and that it will solve all disease,

and that all of this will happen imminently (or at least imminently enough that you have nothing to fear from smoking-related diseases),

and you want to show that you, yes you, are close enough to the action to have come to this conclusion, and you are a true believer,

then a really great way to signal this is to conspicuously take up smoking cigarettes.

Actually I think that smoking cigarettes shows great strength of character.

Or at least that’s the gag I say to my smoking buddies when they light up.

Given everything we know about what smoking does to you, and the relentless, gruesome anti-smoking ad campaigns for years and years, and the smell and the cost and the social shunning and the logistical difficulty of actually finding a legal place to stand, and the easy alternatives like vaping, you must be really independently-minded and strong-willed to stand up to all that and still be on the cigs.

Well done you, I say, well done.

This joke no longer works given the AI flex so I’ll have to stop using it. My friends, thoroughly fed up with me by now, will be relieved.

Another flex:

If your girlfriend isn’t a Chinese honeytrap, does your AI startup even matter?

The story goes that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s extra-marital girlfriend is actually a Chinese spy.

(What’s the benefit to China of her being a spy? Surely not just for lobbying. But to get access to Nvidia GPUs – which her company has been funnelling to Chinese AI labs, it turns out, breaking US export bans. The point being that frontier models can be trained only on cutting edge Nvidia chips, and this is a way for China to keep up, and there is forensic proof that this is what has happened . The second question to ask: why was this disclosed now? We can only guess.)

Rumours of this sort of thing have been bubbling for a while.

Female spies are waging ‘sex warfare’ to steal Silicon Valley secrets , The Times (October 2025). China and Russia are sending attractive women to seduce tech workers…

Even Elon Musk made a gag about it last year: If she’s a 10, you’re an asset.

So if your startup isn’t even worth state-sponsored espionage, why are you bothering.

But if on the other hand you have have mysteriously out-of-your-league hotties (on whatever combination of axes you prefer, they have the psych analysis) sliding into your DMs, and you want to flex that, then heck take them on dates to very fancy, very public restaurants, let everyone notice. Ride the crocodile and watch your pillow talk. You’ll have VCs blowing up your messages, they’ll want in on that.

Remember. It’s only a Chinese honeytrap if she’s from honeytrap province in China otherwise it’s just sparkling industrial espionage.

What makes a flex work is that it is costly in some way.

Like, syphilis sores used to be fashionable :

> the symptoms remained limited to a few painless sores on the genitals and face, which for a time were even a status symbol and indicated that the wearer had had a lot of sexual experience. A sore on the forehead, the ‘Crown of Venus’, was worn with pride.

Another social cost flex, more contemporary, fewer oozing sores: the hierarchy of wristwatches on Wall Street , Business Insider (2016), by OG finance bro anon Goldman Sachs Elevator.

The social signalling and potential faux pas on the ladder of intern, analyst, associate, VP, etc go as you’d expect:

> You’re out of the analyst and associate compensation bands now and starting to make real money. It’s time to go pick up a Rolex Daytona ($12,500) – the quintessential investment banker watch. It’s not that expensive, but there’s an unwritten rule that you can’t have one until you’re at least a VP.

Reading this, you get the sense that everyone is clocking everyone’s wrists like all the time.

But when - if - you make partner, it flips:

> Your Patek Philippe is at home. You gave your Panerai to your deadbeat brother-in-law, and your Rolex Yachtmaster is in the Hamptons. Just as Sam Walton drove a Ford truck and Warren Buffett drives a Lincoln, get yourself a Swatch ($66) like Lloyd Blankfein or a Nike sport swatch ($85) like Hank Paulson. Or better yet, don’t wear one. The power move is to have a few watches stuffed away at home, and then, rarely, if ever, wear one. When you control time, you don’t need to know what time it is.
